content:
The Food and Drug Administration has escalated its response to a Listeria outbreak that has now sickened 46 people — and investigators still have not named the food behind it.

The FDA’s outbreak investigation table, updated October 21 and listed as active under reference number 1417, now shows all three investigative steps checked: traceback, on-site inspection, and sampling. In plain terms, that means the agency is tracing suspected foods through the supply chain, has begun examining a facility, and is collecting and testing products or surfaces. The table states: “FDA has initiated an inspection and sampling.”

But the product column still reads “Not yet identified.” No recall has been announced. And the FDA has not disclosed which facility is being inspected, what is being tested, or where the patients live — which means there is no specific product for families to pull from the refrigerator right now.

The count keeps climbing

The outbreak was added to the FDA table on September 23 with 40 illnesses, when only traceback was under way. The count rose to 44 in early October and now stands at 46. The rise shows illnesses are still being reported, though counts can also grow as states finish laboratory work on older cases.

This is not the only active Listeria investigation. A separate outbreak, reference 1415, added September 30, has 11 cases and also has inspection and sampling under way. A third Listeria investigation, reference 1379, has been marked as ended. The FDA has not said whether any of these outbreaks are connected.

Who is most at risk

Listeria infections are less common than many foodborne illnesses but far more dangerous for certain people. The CDC estimates about 1,250 people are infected and 172 die each year in the United States, making Listeria the fourth leading cause of death from foodborne illness. Pregnant women, newborns, adults 65 and older, and people with weakened immune systems face the greatest risk; in invasive cases not tied to pregnancy, almost 1 in 6 people die, according to the CDC.

Invasive Listeria usually begins within two weeks of eating contaminated food, with fever and flu-like symptoms — plus headache, stiff neck, confusion, loss of balance, or seizures in people who are not pregnant. The illness can be diagnosed with lab tests and treated with antibiotics.

Until the FDA names a source, the practical focus is protection. Public-health guidance for high-risk households includes avoiding unpasteurized dairy, heating deli meats and hot dogs until steaming hot, keeping the refrigerator at 40 degrees Fahrenheit or colder, and cleaning up refrigerator spills promptly. Because Listeria can grow at refrigerator temperatures, leftovers should not be kept too long.

Webb Watch could not confirm any Texas-specific or Webb County cases, because the FDA has not released patient states. This story is informational only — it is not medical advice. Anyone in a high-risk group with symptoms should call a clinician.

title: Listeria Outbreak With No Named Food Reaches 46 Illnesses as FDA Starts On-Site Inspection
